lead: When two columns stand close together, or one sits near a boundary, their separate footings would overlap or spill outside the plot. A combined footing carries both columns on one slab. Its plan follows one rule: put the centroid of the slab under the resultant of the two column loads, so that the soil pressure is uniform. Lengthwise the slab then behaves like an upside-down beam loaded by the soil and supported at the columns; crosswise it is a short cantilever under each column. Two-column footings are common at lift wells, expansion joints and plot edges in city buildings.
prereq: You need the isolated-footing checks of Isolated footings, and shear and bending diagrams for beams.

items: Add the service loads, P = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub>, and find the area A = P/q<sub>s</sub> (plus about 10 % for self-weight when q<sub>s</sub> is a gross value).
Locate the resultant from column 1: x̄ = P<sub>2</sub>s/(P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub>), where s is the column spacing.

Choose the length L so the centre of the slab is at x̄: the projection beyond column 1 is a<sub>1</sub> = L/2 − x̄, and beyond column 2 is a<sub>2</sub> = L − s − a<sub>1</sub>. Then B = A/L (or fix B and find L = A/B).
If a boundary limits a<sub>1</sub> (say a<sub>1</sub> = 0), L follows from L = 2x̄; if even that is impossible, use a trapezoidal footing or a strap footing.

blocks.text: With the centroid under the resultant, the factored soil pressure is uniform: q<sub>u</sub> = (P<sub>u1</sub> + P<sub>u2</sub>)/(LB), and the line load along the footing is w = q<sub>u</sub>B.
Draw the shear force and bending moment diagrams of a beam of length L carrying the upward line load w and the two downward column loads. Measuring x from the end beyond column 1:
V(x) = w x − P<sub>u1</sub>[x > a<sub>1</sub>] − P<sub>u2</sub>[x > a<sub>1</sub> + s];  M(x) = w x²/2 − P<sub>u1</sub>(x − a<sub>1</sub>) − P<sub>u2</sub>(x − a<sub>1</sub> − s)
blocks.where: a term in brackets counts only once x has passed that column; M positive means tension at the bottom.

items: Under each column (the cantilevers) the moment is sagging: tension at the bottom.
Between the columns the soil pushes the slab up between two supports, so it hogs: tension at the top. The largest hogging moment is where V = 0, at x = Pu1/w.

Depth is set by one-way shear at d from a column face (and checked for punching under the heavier column); footings carry shear by concrete, so a deeper slab is the usual answer. Steel: bottom bars for the largest sagging moment, top bars for the hogging moment, each at least 0.12 % of the gross section.

blocks.text: Across the width the column load spreads out to the edges, so a strip under each column works as a cantilever of length (B − b)/2 from the column face, loaded by P<sub>u</sub>/B per metre of width. Codes do not fix the width of this strip; a common choice is the column width plus d on each side. Its bottom bars sit above the longitudinal bottom bars, so their effective depth is one bar diameter less. Elsewhere, nominal transverse steel (0.12 %) is enough.

examples.question: Two 400 mm square columns, 3.0 m apart, carry service loads of 600 kN and 900 kN. The safe bearing capacity is 150 kN/m² (net) and the footing width is fixed at 2.0 m. Design the rectangular combined footing in M20 concrete with Fe415 bars.
steps: Resultant from the 600 kN column: x̄ = 900 × 3/1500 = 1.80 m. Projections: a<sub>1</sub> = 2.5 − 1.80 = 0.70 m and a<sub>2</sub> = 5.0 − 3.0 − 0.70 = 1.30 m.
Factored loads 900 and 1350 kN; q<sub>u</sub> = 2250/(5 × 2) = 225 kN/m²; w = 225 × 2.0 = 450 kN/m.
Shear: V = 315 kN just left of column 1 and -585 kN just right; V = 0 at x = 900/450 = 2.00 m; 765 kN just left of column 2 and -585 kN just right; zero at the far end.
Moments: 110.25 kN·m (sagging) under column 1; 270 kN·m hogging at x = 2.0 m; 380.25 kN·m sagging under column 2 (centre values, slightly on the safe side).

Depth: one-way shear governs. Adopt D = 700 mm, d = 700 − 50 − 8 = 642 mm. The largest shear at d from a face is left of column 2: V<sub>u</sub> = 386.1 kN, τ<sub>v</sub> = 386100/(2000 × 642) = 0.301 N/mm².
Bottom steel for 380 kN·m: A<sub>st</sub> = 1686 mm², just above the minimum 0.0012 × 2000 × 700 = 1680 mm²; provide 9 bars of 16 mm = 1810 mm².

Top steel for 270 kN·m: A<sub>st</sub> = 1188 mm², below the minimum, so 9 bars would do for bending. But the governing shear section (2.86 m from the end) has a hogging moment of 104 kN·m, so the top bars are its tension steel: 9 bars give p<sub>t</sub> = 0.141 % and τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.280 < 0.301 N/mm². Provide 12 bars of 16 mm = 2413 mm², p<sub>t</sub> = 0.188 %, τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.310 N/mm² ≥ τ<sub>v</sub>.
Punching at the 1350 kN column: V<sub>u</sub> = 1350 − 225 × (1.042)² = 1105.7 kN, b<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 1042 = 4168 mm, τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.413 ≤ 1.118 N/mm².

Transverse under column 2: cantilever (2.0 − 0.4)/2 = 0.8 m, load 1350/2.0 = 675 kN/m, M<sub>u</sub> = 675 × 0.8²/2 = 216 kN·m on a strip 0.4 + 2 × 0.642 = 1.68 m wide, d = 626 mm: A<sub>st</sub> = 974 mm², minimum 1415 mm²: 8 bars of 16 mm. Under column 1: 144 kN·m, 8 bars of 16 mm.
examples.answer: Footing 5.0 m × 2.0 m × 700 mm, projections 0.70 m and 1.30 m; 9 bars of 16 mm at the bottom and 12 at the top lengthwise (the top bars raised for shear); 8 and 8 transverse 16 mm bars under the heavy and light columns; all shear checks pass.

traps: Putting the slab centre midway between the columns when the loads differ. The centre must sit under the resultant.
Missing the top steel between the columns, where the slab hogs.
Taking the hogging moment at mid-span. Its largest value is where the shear is zero, here 1.3 m from column 1, not 1.5 m.
Sizing the area with factored loads, or the depth with service pressure.
Designing only lengthwise: each column also needs transverse bottom bars.

quiz.q: State the condition that makes the soil pressure under a combined footing uniform.
quiz.a: The centroid of the footing area must lie on the line of action of the resultant of the column loads.

quiz.q: Why is the steel between the columns at the top?
quiz.a: Between the columns the upward soil pressure bends the slab upward between two supports, like a beam turned upside down, so the top face is in tension.

quiz.q: Two columns carry 400 kN and 800 kN, 3 m apart; q<sub>s</sub> = 120 kN/m² and B = 2 m. Find L and both projections.
For the worked example, find the hogging moment at mid-way between the columns (x = 2.2 m).
quiz.a: M = 450 × 2.2²/2 − 900 × (2.2 − 0.7) = 1089 − 1350 = -261 kN·m (hogging 261), less than the 270 kN·m at the zero-shear point.

quiz.q: In the apply question above, the designer centres the footing midway (2.5 m from the 400 kN column). What pressures result?
quiz.a: e = 2.5 − 2.0 = 0.5 m; M = 1200 × 0.5 = 600 kN·m; Z = 2 × 5²/6 = 8.333 m³; p = 120 ± 72 = 192 and 48 kN/m². The heavy end exceeds 120 kN/m², so the footing is unsafe.

quiz.q: If the spacing in the worked example grows to 5 m with the same loads and B = 2 m, can the same 5 m long footing work?
quiz.a: x̄ = 900 × 5/1500 = 3.0 m, so a<sub>1</sub> = 2.5 − 3.0 = −0.5 m: the centroid would fall beyond column 1. Make it narrower and longer (B = 1.5 m, L = 6.67 m gives a<sub>1</sub> = 0.33 m, a<sub>2</sub> = 1.33 m) or use a strap footing.

beyond: Not for the exam. When the space between columns is too small even for a combined slab, designers use a strap (cantilever) footing: two pads joined by a stiff beam that balances the eccentric one. Rows of columns end up on strip or raft foundations analysed as beams or plates on elastic foundations. Search for "strap footing design", "trapezoidal combined footing" and "beam on elastic foundation".

figure.caption: The worked example’s combined footing, 5.0 m long and 2.0 m wide, under factored column loads of 900 kN and 1350 kN, with the upward line load of 450 kN/m. The shear is zero 2.0 m from the left end, where the hogging moment of 270 kN·m puts tension at the top; the sagging moments under the columns are 110.3 and 380.3 kN·m (kN and kN·m).
